Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

title: Midterm 2 study guide
text:
Learning outcomes (Lectures 18–29)

Light review — Quiz 5 / basis (Lecture 14)

Explain what a basis accomplishes and what dimension means.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use span, independence, basis, and dimension accurately when they reappear with matrices (column space, null space, rank).



Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects

Identify matrix dimensions, rows, columns, and entries.
Represent datasets, networks, images, or systems as matrices.
Perform matrix addition, scaling, and transposition.
Recognize zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and sparse matrices.
Explain one practical consequence of matrix structure.



Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication

Compute \(Ax\) by hand for a small matrix.
Interpret \(Ax\) as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\).
Interpret \(A\) as an input-output transformation.
Explain how the dimensions of \(A\) determine the input and output spaces.



Lecture 20 — Transforming space

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.

From October 19 through the midterm, class meetings are Lectures 21–31. The bullets below are grouped by those lecture numbers. Nothing from the old lists was removed; systems and elimination share Lecture 21, RREF and one-step dynamics share Lecture 22, and iteration and long-run patterns share Lecture 23.


Lecture 21 — Systems, elimination, and \(Ax=b\)

Translate equations or contextual constraints into \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) belongs to the span of the columns of \(A\).
Classify systems as square, underdetermined, or overdetermined.
Anticipate circumstances producing zero, one, or many solutions.



Lecture 21, continued — Gaussian elimination

Perform elementary row operations.
Match each row operation with the elementary matrix that performs it.
Reduce a small augmented matrix to echelon form, including by left-multiplying those matrices.
Solve a small system using back substitution.
Explain why row operations preserve the solution set.



Lecture 22 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software

Interpret reduced row echelon form.
Identify pivot and free variables.
Describe a solution set parametrically.
Distinguish inconsistent, unique, and infinite-solution cases.
Use software to solve or row-reduce a system and verify with a residual.



Lecture 22, continued — Linear dynamical systems

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.



Lecture 23 — Iteration, simulation, and long-run behavior

Simulate many time steps computationally.
Plot state components through time.
Recognize stabilization, growth, decay, or oscillation.
Conduct a simple what-if simulation.
State limitations of a linear dynamical model.



Lecture 23, continued — Predict a system through time

Implement a linear dynamical model.
Write or complete a short iterative calculation.
Validate the first steps by hand.
Compare results under altered parameters or initial states.
Record an unexplained long-run pattern for later investigation (eigenvalues come later).



Lecture 23 — Matrix products and powers

Determine whether a product is defined and give its dimensions; compute a small product.
Interpret \(ABx\) as a sequence of transformations; note \(AB\neq BA\) in general.
Connect \(A^k x\) to repeated dynamics.



Lab 3 — Computational cost and solve syntax

Distinguish storage, processing work, and wall-clock time.
Count ops on a small elimination; recognize \(O(n^3)\) scaling (doubling \(n\) \(\approx\times 8\)).
Solve \(Ax=b\) in software and check the residual; compute a small matrix power.



Lecture 24 — Inverses from elementary matrices

Explain \(A^{-1}\) as the product of elementary matrices that reduce \(A\) to \(I\).
Compute inverses via \([A\mid I]\) and the \(2\times 2\) formula.
Connect invertibility to unique solvability of \(Ax=b\) for every \(b\).



Lecture 25 — Rank, column space, null space

Interpret column space and null space through \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax=0\).
Determine rank from pivots or independent columns.
Find simple bases for column or null spaces.
Connect rank to consistency, independence, and dimension.
Use subspace, basis, dimension, rank, column space, and null space correctly.



Lecture 26 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.
Connect determinants to the coming characteristic equation (preview only).

text:
Same pantry, two meal targets
You are planning meals from two foods only:

\(x_1\) = number of servings of oats
\(x_2\) = number of servings of yogurt

Each serving contributes (toy numbers, not a real diet plan):




Protein (g)
Fiber (g)




1 serving oats
2
1


1 serving yogurt
3
1



So if you eat \(x_1\) oats and \(x_2\) yogurt, the total protein and fiber are \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{protein} &= 2x_1 + 3x_2,\\
\text{fiber} &= 1x_1 + 1x_2.
\end{aligned}
\] In matrix form that is \(Ax=b\), where \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}\text{protein target}\\\text{fiber target}\end{bmatrix}.
\] The pantry (matrix \(A\)) stays the same every day. What changes is the target vector \(b\) — how much protein and fiber you want that day.
C3.1 — Monday. You want 26 g protein and 10 g fiber.
How many servings of oats and yogurt should you eat?
Write \(b\), solve \(Ax=b\) with the one-liner (A \ b / solve), and check with \(Ax-b\) (should be near zero).
Expected: \(b=(26,10)\), \(x=(4,6)\) — 4 oats, 6 yogurt.
C3.2 — Tuesday. Same two foods (same \(A\)). Today you want 31 g protein and 12 g fiber.
How many servings of each? Solve \(Ax'=b'\) and check \(Ax'-b'\).
Expected: \(b'=(31,12)\), \(x'=(5,7)\).
Pause. You solved two systems that share the same \(A\) and differ only in \(b\). Was calling the one-liner twice the smartest use of work? What information about \(A\) could a computer reuse on Tuesday instead of starting over?

title: Lab 3 — Nutrients, LU, and Lab 2’s algorithm on the machine
text:
First factorization: \(A=LU\)

From Lab 2’s \(E_i\) to two triangular factors
Lab 2 cleared below pivots by left-multiplying elementary matrices \(E_i\). Stop when \(A\) is upper triangular — call that matrix \(U\). Do not scale pivots to \(1\) or clear above (that is RREF / inverse territory).
For the nutrient matrix, one step does it. Subtract \(\tfrac12\) times row 1 from row 2: \[
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-\tfrac12&1\end{bmatrix}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
EA=U=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\0&-\tfrac12\end{bmatrix}.
\] So \(EA=U\). Multiply on the left by \(E^{-1}\): \[
A=E^{-1}U.
\] The inverse of “subtract \(\tfrac12\cdot\)(row 1) from row 2” is “add \(\tfrac12\cdot\)(row 1) to row 2”: \[
E^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\\tfrac12&1\end{bmatrix}=L
\] (lower triangular; the multiplier \(\tfrac12\) sits where we cleared). Thus \[
A=LU.
\]
Larger \(n\) (same idea, more \(E_i\)). Clearing below the pivots is a product \[
E_k\cdots E_2 E_1 A = U
\] (upper triangular). Those \(E_i\) are the “go down to \(U\)” group. Invert and reverse order: \[
A = \underbrace{E_1^{-1}E_2^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}}_{L} U.
\] Each \(E_i^{-1}\) puts the multiplier back (same spot, opposite sign), so \(L\) is lower triangular with \(1\)s on the diagonal. A second group of elementary matrices (scale pivots to \(1\), clear above) would finish RREF / \([A\mid I]\) — solvers usually skip that group when they only need \(x\).


Using \(LU\) to solve \(Ax=b\)
If \(A=LU\), then \(Ax=b\) means \(LUx=b\). Introduce \(y=Ux\):

Forward substitution: solve \(Ly=b\) for \(y\) (easy: \(L\) lower triangular).
Back substitution: solve \(Ux=y\) for \(x\) (easy: \(U\) upper triangular).

Same \(L\) and \(U\) work for every new \(b\) (Monday, Tuesday, …). Factor once; each day is two triangular solves.
C3.3.

Form \(L\) and \(U\) for the nutrient \(A\); check \(LU=A\).

For Monday’s \(b=(26,10)\), solve \(Ly=b\), then \(Ux=y\), by hand or in software. Check that \(x\) matches C3.1.

Behind A \ b (part 1). A typical dense solver does this bookkeeping (often with row swaps: \(PA=LU\) if a pivot is \(0\)/tiny). This nutrient \(A\) needs no swap. Full RREF every time would redo extra work you do not need for one \(x\).







Goal

Many \(Ax=b\) (same foods, new targets)
\(A=LU\), then \(Ly=b\), \(Ux=y\) — close to what A \ b reuses


Undo map for every \(b\)
\([A\mid I]\to A^{-1}\) (extra \(E_i\) group) — useful, but usually not how A \ b works

section: Bridge from Lab 2: program the algorithm (no zero pivots)
text:
Bridge from Lab 2: program the algorithm (no zero pivots)
Lab 2 listed an algorithm while every pivot is nonzero, and walked a \(3\times 3\) system by hand to echelon (then sketched full RREF). Today: put that algorithm on the machine and push all the way to RREF (pivots \(=1\), zeros above and below).
Reuse Lab 2’s system: \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\2&3&1\\1&2&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}6\\11\\14\end{bmatrix},\qquad
M=[A\mid b]\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 4}.
\] (You already know the answer will be \(x=(1,2,3)\).)

Pattern for one step
Pivot at position \((k,k)\) (1-based). To clear entry \((i,k)\): \[
c=\frac{M_{ik}}{M_{kk}},\qquad
E = I_3\text{ with }{-c}\text{ in row }i,\text{ column }k,\qquad
M \leftarrow EM.
\] To make the pivot \(1\): scale row \(k\) by \(1/M_{kk}\) (elementary matrix = \(I\) with that factor on the diagonal).
C3.4 — Run RREF (nonzero pivots). Copy–paste one of the blocks below, run it, and watch \(M\) become \([I\mid x]\). Then compare to the one-liner on the same \(A,b\).
For each pivot column \(k\): scale the pivot to \(1\) with an elementary matrix, then clear every other entry in that column the same way (Lab 2’s \(E\), left-multiply, replace \(M\)).
Octave (copy all):
A = [1 1 1; 2 3 1; 1 2 3];
b = [6; 11; 14];
M = [A b];          % 3x4 augmented matrix
n = 3;

% for k = 1:n ... end  →  repeat with k = 1, then 2, then 3
for k = 1:n
  % M(k,k) = entry in row k, column k (1-based)
  E = eye(n);
  E(k,k) = 1 / M(k,k);   % put the scale factor on the diagonal of E
  M = E * M;
  % disp prints; num2str(k) turns k into text for the message
  disp(["after scale pivot ", num2str(k)]); disp(M);

  for i = 1:n
    if i == k
      continue;          % skip the pivot row itself
    end
    E = eye(n);
    E(i,k) = -M(i,k);    % -c in row i, column k
    M = E * M;
  end
  disp(["after clear column ", num2str(k)]); disp(M);
end

x = M(:, end)            % all rows (:), last column (end) = solution
x_solver = A \ b
residual = A * x - b
Python (copy all):
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1., 1, 1],
              [2, 3, 1],
              [1, 2, 3]])
b = np.array([6., 11, 14])
M = np.column_stack((A, b))  # 3x4 augmented matrix
n = 3

# for k in range(n):  →  k = 0, then 1, then 2  (0-based)
for k in range(n):
    # M[k, k] = entry in row k, column k (0-based)
    E = np.eye(n)
    E[k, k] = 1.0 / M[k, k]  # put the scale factor on the diagonal of E
    M = E @ M
    print(f"after scale pivot {k+1}\n", M)  # f-string inserts k+1 into the text

    for i in range(n):
        if i == k:
            continue          # skip the pivot row itself
        E = np.eye(n)
        E[i, k] = -M[i, k]    # -c in row i, column k
        M = E @ M
    print(f"after clear column {k+1}\n", M)

x = M[:, -1]                  # all rows (:), last column (-1) = solution
print("x from RREF:", x)
print("x from solve:", np.linalg.solve(A, b))
print("residual:", A @ x - b)
Expected: final \(M=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&|&1\\0&1&0&|&2\\0&0&1&|&3\end{bmatrix}\), so \(x=(1,2,3)\) — matching A \ b / solve, residual \(\approx 0\).
Behind A\b (part 2). Your coded RREF is the Lab 2 algorithm made explicit. Production solvers usually stop earlier (LU / \(PA=LU\), then triangular solves) instead of forming full RREF every time — same family of row operations, better bookkeeping when only \(b\) changes.

title: Lab 3 — Nutrients, LU, and Lab 2’s algorithm on the machine
text:
Same algorithm, \(I\) instead of \(b\)
Replace the right-hand column by an identity: form the \(3\times 6\) matrix \([A\mid I]\). Run the same elementary updates until the left block is \(I\). Call the right \(3\times 3\) block \(B\).
C3.5.

Obtain \(B\). Check \(B*A\) / B @ A equals \(I\) (within rounding).

Check \(B*b\) equals the \(x\) from C3.4 — so \(x=Bb\) also works.

\(B\) is the product of all the elementary matrices you left-multiplied so we’ve saved the whole reduction as one matrix.

One sentence: why solvers still prefer A\b / LU over “form \(B=A^{-1}\), then \(Bb\)” for a single (or few) right-hand side(s).

Expected: \(BA=I\), \(Bb=x\). Monday’s name for \(B\) is \(A^{-1}\). Forming \(A^{-1}\) does extra work when you only need one \(x\).

title: Lab 6 — Fit and Compress
text:
Ops strip
Fit a line \(y\approx c_1+c_2 t\) to points \((t,y)=(0,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,2)\).
C6.0. Build \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) and \(b=(1,2,2)\). Solve for \(\hat c\) with least squares (A\b / lstsq). Print \(\hat c\) and the residual \(\|A\hat c-b\|\).
Expected: \(\hat c=(7/6,1/2)\) (about \((1.167,0.5)\)); residual about \(0.408\).
C6.0b (bridge). Compute the SVD of this same \(A\). Spot-check that the first two left singular vectors (columns of \(U\)) look orthonormal: products \(\approx 0\) off-diagonal, norms \(\approx 1\) (Lecture 14 vocabulary; Lecture 40 bridge). No need to rebuild \(\hat c\) by hand from \(\Sigma\) — just notice SVD is the orthonormal toolkit behind a sturdy LS solve.
Expected: \(u_i^{\mathsf{T}}u_j\approx 0\) (\(i\neq j\)), \(\|u_i\|\approx 1\).

title: Lab 6 — Fit and Compress
text:
Application
Work with the \(4\times 4\) matrix \[
M=\begin{bmatrix}
4&2&2&0\\
2&4&0&2\\
2&0&4&2\\
0&2&2&4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
C6.1. Compute the SVD of \(M\). List the singular values (largest to smallest).
Expected: singular values \(8,4,4,0\) (or equivalent ordering with a zero).
C6.2. Build the rank-\(k=1\) approximation \(M_1\) and the rank-\(k=2\) approximation \(M_2\). Report \(\|M-M_k\|_F\) for each \(k\).
Expected: residual drops when \(k\) goes from \(1\) to \(2\) (exact numbers depend on rounding; \(k=2\) should be clearly smaller).
C6.3. Storage: for an \(m\times n\) matrix, truncated SVD stores about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers. For this \(4\times4\) matrix, compute \(k(m+n+1)\) for \(k=1\) and \(k=2\). For a \(100\times 100\) grayscale image, which \(k\) values stay under half of \(100\cdot 100=10000\) entries?
Expected: here \(k(4+4+1)=9k\), so \(9\) and \(18\). For \(100\times 100\), \(k(201)<5000\) ⇒ \(k\le 24\).

Learning objectives

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Fill in
A linear system with \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns can be written \(Ax=b\), where \(A\) is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\), \(x\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector, and \(b\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector.
Column view. Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of the columns of \(A\)? Equivalently: does \(b\) lie in \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\)?
Shape vocabulary (compare \(m\) equations to \(n\) unknowns):








Name
Relation
Typical intuition




Square
\(m=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often one solution, but not always


Overdetermined
\(m>\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (too many constraints)


Underdetermined
\(m<\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (free variables)



These are tendencies, not guarantees. A square system can be inconsistent or have infinitely many solutions. An overdetermined system can still be consistent.
Possible outcomes for \(Ax=b\):

No solution — \(b\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) the column space.
Unique solution — \(b\) is in the column space in exactly \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) way.
Infinitely many solutions — \(b\) is in the column space in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) ways (free parameters).

The augmented matrix of \(Ax=b\) is \([A\mid b]\), with \(b\) as an extra \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
Elementary row operations that do not change the solution set:

\(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\) two rows.
Multiply a row by a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) scalar. (Multiplying by \(0\) is not allowed: it is not reversible and can destroy an equation.)
Add a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of one row to another row.

Matrices for those operations. Left-multiplying \([A\mid b]\) by a matrix does the row operation. Build that matrix by doing the same operation to \(I\). For two equations:
Swap the two rows: \[
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Multiply row 1 by \(c\neq 0\), or multiply row 2 by \(c\neq 0\): \[
\begin{bmatrix}c&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&c\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(c\) times row 1 to row 2, or add \(c\) times row 2 to row 1: \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\c&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1&c\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The extra number sits in the row you are changing, in the column of the row you copy from. For three equations, start from \(I_3\) and edit that same spot. Adding \(2\) times row 1 to row 3 uses \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\2&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Why they preserve solutions: each allowed operation is reversible, so the new system is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) to the old one. Each matrix above is invertible, which is the same fact in matrix language.
Gaussian elimination aims for echelon form: zeros \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) each pivot, pivots marching right as you go down. Then back substitution solves from the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) equation upward. Reduced form, free variables, and software are next time.

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Worked in class
W1. Matrix form. Three unknowns \(x_1,x_2,x_3\): \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_2 &= 4 \\
x_2 - x_3 &= 1 \\
2x_1 + x_3 &= 3.
\end{aligned}
\] Write \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\). Square / over / under?
W2. Span interpretation. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\end{bmatrix},\quad
c=\begin{bmatrix}3\\5\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Are the columns of \(A\) independent? Describe \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns}\}\). (b) Does \(Ax=b\) have a solution? Infinitely many? (c) Does \(Ax=c\) have a solution?
W3. Eliminate and back-substitute. Starting from \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 3 & | & 8
\end{bmatrix},
\] replace Row 2 by (Row 2) \(-\) \(2\cdot\)(Row 1). Solve for \(x_2\), then \(x_1\).
W4. Three operations, then a full solve by applying matrices. Start from the warm-up matrix \[
M=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&|&3\\2&1&|&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Swap the two rows: \[
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}M
=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&|&1\\1&-2&|&3\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Multiply row 1 by \(2\): \[
\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}M
=\begin{bmatrix}2&-4&|&6\\2&1&|&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(-2\) times row 1 to row 2. This is the elimination step: \[
E_1=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-2&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E_1 M=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&|&3\\0&5&|&-5\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Continue from \(E_1 M\) until the left side is \(I\). Multiply the new row 2 by \(\frac{1}{5}\): \[
E_2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&\frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E_2 E_1 M=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&|&3\\0&1&|&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(2\) times the new row 2 to row 1: \[
E_3=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E_3 E_2 E_1 M=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&|&1\\0&1&|&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Read the solution \(x=(1,-1)\). The same three matrices clear \(A\) itself: \(E_3 E_2 E_1 A=I\). We name that product \(A^{-1}\) later.
W5 (if time). Anticipating outcomes. Without fully solving, say what you expect (and why):

\(2\) equations, \(2\) unknowns, with clearly parallel incompatible lines.
\(1\) equation, \(3\) unknowns: \(x_1+x_2+x_3=5\).
\(3\) equations, \(2\) unknowns that happen to be consistent (the third is the sum of the first two).

W6 (if time). Context \(\to Ax=b\). Two foods (oats, yogurt) and two nutrients (protein, fiber). Per serving: oats give \(2\) g protein and \(1\) g fiber; yogurt gives \(3\) g protein and \(1\) g fiber. Monday’s targets: \(26\) g protein and \(10\) g fiber. Write the two equations and the matrix form \(Ax=b\). Square? (Preview of Lab 3.)
W7 (if time). A \(3\times 3\) echelon. Reduce \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & | & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 1 & 0 & | & 5
\end{bmatrix}
\] to echelon form and decide whether a solution exists.

text:

Y1. Write as \(Ax=b\): \[

Y2. Let \(A\) have columns \(a_1=(1,0,1)\) and \(a_2=(0,1,1)\). For \(b=(1,1,2)\), explain in one sentence why \(Ax=b\) has a solution, and give one solution \(x\).

Y4. A sensor gives \(4\) linear measurements for \(2\) unknown parameters. Is the system typically overdetermined? Does that guarantee inconsistency?
Y5. Augmented matrix for \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - x_2 &= 1 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2 &= 12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Y6. Clear the \((2,1)\) entry of \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\] by a row replacement. Write the new matrix.
Y7. From the echelon form \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix},
\] solve by back substitution.
Y8. True or false, with a one-line reason: if you swap two rows of \([A\mid b]\), the solution set of \(Ax=b\) can change.
Y9. Write the \(2\times 2\) elementary matrix for each operation.

Multiply row 1 by \(4\).
Add \(3\) times row 2 to row 1.
Apply the matrix from (b) to \(\begin{bmatrix}1&0&|&2\\0&1&|&5\end{bmatrix}\).







NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\1&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}0\\7\end{bmatrix}.
\] Square (\(m=n=2\)).
Y2. \(b=1\cdot a_1+1\cdot a_2\), so \(b\) is in the column span; one solution is \(x=(1,1)\).
Y3. False. Square systems can be inconsistent (parallel lines) or have infinitely many solutions (the same line twice).
Y4. Typically overdetermined (\(m=4>n=2\)). No — consistency depends on whether \(b\) lands in the column space.
Y5. \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y6. Row2 \(\leftarrow\) Row2 \(-\) \(3\cdot\)Row1 gives \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y7. From Row 2: \(5x_2=9\) so \(x_2=9/5\). From Row 1: \(x_1-x_2=1\) so \(x_1=1+9/5=14/5\). Solution \(x=(14/5,\,9/5)\).
Y8. False. Swapping rows reorders equations and keeps the same solution set.
Y9. (a) \(\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) \(\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (c) Row 1 becomes \((1,0,2)+3(0,1,5)=(1,3,17)\), so \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&3&|&17\\0&1&|&5\end{bmatrix}.
\]

text:
Warm-up

title: Lecture 24 — Inverses from elementary matrices
text:
Fill in

Inverse from elementary matrices
A square matrix \(A\) is invertible if there exist elementary matrices \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\) (row operations) with \[
E_k\cdots E_2 E_1 A = \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}.
\] We then define \[
A^{-1} := E_k\cdots E_2 E_1.
\] So \(A^{-1}A=I\). (When \(A\) is invertible one also gets \(AA^{-1}=I\).)
Meaning. Each \(E_i\) undoes / performs one reversible row operation. Their product undoes the whole map \(x\mapsto Ax\): if \(y=Ax\), then \(A^{-1}y=x\).
Solving — why the inverse is powerful. If \(A\) is invertible and \(Ax=b\), then \[
x = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] The point of \(A^{-1}\) is generality: you build one matrix that works for any right-hand side. Change \(b\), keep the same \(A^{-1}\), multiply again. Equivalently: \(Ax=b\) has a unique solution for every \(b\) iff \(A\) is invertible.
(Elimination on \([A\mid b]\) still finds one \(x\) for one \(b\). The inverse is the packaged “undo everything” map.)
Same \(E_i\), two packages (Lab 3). Stopping elimination at an upper-triangular \(U\) gives a factorization \(A=LU\) — great for solving many systems with the same \(A\). Pushing all the way to \(I\) on \([A\mid I]\) builds \(A^{-1}\) — great for the undo map. Software’s A\b is closer to the LU idea than to forming \(A^{-1}\) first.


Practical computation
To find \(A^{-1}\) by elimination, form the wide matrix \([A\mid I]\) and row-reduce until the left block is \(I\) (when possible). The right block is then \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
For \(2\times 2\), that procedure yields a closed formula (next). For \(3\times 3\), do the elimination by hand on \([A\mid I]\).
Check. Always verify \(A^{-1}A=I\) (or \(AA^{-1}=I\)) on a candidate.
When it fails. If a zero row appears on the left while reducing \([A\mid I]\), you cannot reach \(I\): \(A\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) inverse. (Columns are dependent; \(Ax=0\) has a nontrivial solution.)

title: Lecture 24 — Inverses from elementary matrices
text:
Worked in class
W1. Product of \(E_i\) is the inverse. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Write the elementary matrix \(E\) that subtracts \(2\) times row 2 from row 1 (after you already have a pivot \(1\) in position \((2,2)\) — or clear the \((1,2)\) entry of \(A\) directly). Check \(EA=I\).

Conclude \(A^{-1}=E\) and write \(A^{-1}\) explicitly.

W2. Derive the \(2\times 2\) formula. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}
\] with \(ad-bc\neq 0\). Reduce \([A\mid I]\) to \([I\mid A^{-1}]\) (or clear systematically with elementary matrices) and show \[
A^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}.
\] (We will call \(ad-bc\) the determinant on Friday.)
W3. Use the formula. Compute \(A^{-1}\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}
\] using W2. Check \(A^{-1}A=I\).
W4. Another \(2\times 2\). Find \(A^{-1}\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}
\] by the formula, then check \(AA^{-1}=I\).
W5. \(3\times 3\) by elimination. Form \([A\mid I]\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\] and reduce the left block to \(I\). Read \(A^{-1}\) from the right block. Check \(A^{-1}A=I\).
W6. No inverse. Try the same method for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\] What goes wrong in \([A\mid I]\)? Connect to \(Ax=0\) or dependent columns.
W7. When does an inverse exist? For square \(A\), list equivalent ideas (any three):

can reduce \(A\) to \(I\) by elementary matrices
\(A^{-1}\) exists
\(Ax=b\) has a unique solution for every \(b\)
\(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution
columns of \(A\) are independent
(Friday) \(\det A\neq 0\)

W8. Same inverse, two right-hand sides. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix},
\] form \(A^{-1}\) (formula). Then compute \(x=A^{-1}b\) for \[
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
b'=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Check \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax'=b'\). Same \(A^{-1}\), two different answers — that is the “general undo” idea.

title: Lecture 24 — Inverses from elementary matrices
text:
Your turn
Y1. Using elementary matrices / \([A\mid I]\), find \(A^{-1}\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Check \(A^{-1}A=I\).
Y2. Use the \(2\times 2\) formula on \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}
\] (\(90^\circ\) CCW). What geometric map is \(A^{-1}\)?
Y3. Reduce \([A\mid I]\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\] and read \(A^{-1}\). Check one of \(A^{-1}A\) or \(AA^{-1}\).
Y4. Does \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}
\] have an inverse? Explain using \([A\mid I]\) or \(Ax=b\).
Y5. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(A\) is invertible, then for every \(b\) the system \(Ax=b\) has exactly one solution.
Y6. True or false, with a one-line reason: if you already know \(A^{-1}\), you can solve \(Ax=b\) for a new \(b\) without redoing elimination on \(A\) — just multiply \(A^{-1}b\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Clear the \((1,2)\) entry: \(E=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) gives \(EA=I\), so \[
A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Check: \(A^{-1}A=I\).
Y2. \(ad-bc=1\), so \[
A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}
\] (rotation \(90^\circ\) clockwise). Check: \(A^{-1}A=I\).
Y3. \([A\mid I]\) reduces to right block \[
A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\] (subtract \(2\) times row 1 from row 2 on the wide matrix). Check: \(A^{-1}A=I\).
Y4. No. Left block of \([A\mid I]\) gets a zero row; cannot reach \(I\). Equivalently \(Ax=(0,1)\) has no solution, or \(Ax=0\) has nontrivial solutions such as \((0,1)\).
Y5. True. Invertibility means \(x=A^{-1}b\) is the unique solution for every \(b\).
Y6. True. That is the point of \(A^{-1}\): one general undo for every \(b\).

title: Lecture 25 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Are the three columns independent? (Look carefully at columns 1 and 2.)
For which \(b\) can \(Ax=b\) have a solution — any \(b\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), or only some?

title: Lecture 25 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Fill in
The column space \(C(A)\) is the span of the columns of \(A\). Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\)?
The null space \(N(A)\) is the set of solutions of \(Ax=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\). It always contains \(0\); nontrivial null vectors mean dependent columns.
A subspace is a nonempty set closed under addition and scaling. Both \(C(A)\) and \(N(A)\) are subspaces.
A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. The dimension of a subspace is the number of vectors in any basis.
The rank of \(A\) is \[
\operatorname{rank}(A) = \underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}
\] (equivalently: number of pivot columns after elimination / RREF). Then \[
\dim C(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A),\qquad \dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)
\] for an \(m\times n\) matrix (number of free variables \(=\) nullity).
Reading RREF for bases.

Pivot columns of the original \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\).
Free-variable special solutions form a basis for \(N(A)\).







NoteEnrichment (not on quizzes)



Strang’s other two subspaces: the row space \(C(A^{\mathsf{T}})\) and left nullspace \(N(A^{\mathsf{T}})\). Same rank story; we do not drill them for Quiz 10 / Midterm 2.

title: Lecture 25 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Worked in class
W1. Column space via \(Ax=b\). Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\) in words. Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Is \(b=(1,3,0)\)?
W2. Null space. Same \(A\). Solve \(Ax=0\). Give a basis for \(N(A)\) (it may be \(\{0\}\) only — say so).
W3. Rank from pivots. The RREF of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\] is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)? Which columns of the original \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\).
W4. Dictionary. Match each phrase to the right idea: consistency of \(Ax=b\); uniqueness of the solution when it exists; “how big is the column space?”

title: Lecture 25 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 \\
-1 & -2 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and a basis for \(C(A)\). Is \(b=(2,-2,0)\) in \(C(A)\)?
Y2. For the same \(A\), find a basis for \(N(A)\). How many free variables?
Y3. True or false: if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix with \(m\ge n\), then \(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution.
Y4. True or false: row space and left nullspace will appear on Quiz 10.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Columns: \(a_2=2a_1\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=1\). Basis for \(C(A)\): \(\{(1,-1,0)\}\) (or any nonzero multiple). Yes — \(b=2a_1\).
Y2. \(Ax=0\) means \(x_1+2x_2=0\), so \(x=(-2t,\,t)=t(-2,1)\). Basis for \(N(A)\): \(\{(-2,1)\}\). One free variable; \(\dim N(A)=1=2-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
Y3. True. Full column rank means no free variables, so \(N(A)=\{0\}\).
Y4. False. Enrichment only — not quiz material.

Learning objectives

title: Lecture 26 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What does \(x\mapsto Ax\) do to the unit square? What is the area of the image?
Are the columns of \(B\) independent? Guess whether \(B\) is invertible.

title: Lecture 26 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Fill in
For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\), \[
\det A = ad-bc.
\] Geometrically, \(|\det A|\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) scaling factor of the unit square under \(x\mapsto Ax\) (signed area encodes orientation).
Triangular / diagonal. If \(T\) is upper or lower triangular (including diagonal), \[
\det T = \underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}.
\]
Invertibility. For square \(A\): \[
A\text{ invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det A \neq \underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}.
\] If \(\det A=0\), the image of the unit cube/square is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (lost dimension): columns are dependent, \(Ax=b\) fails for some \(b\), and \(N(A)\) is nontrivial.
Product rule (preview). \(\det(AB)=(\det A)(\det B)\). Useful later for compositions.
Coming attraction. Eigenvalues solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) — the characteristic equation. Today’s \(\det\) is the tool; Week 13 builds the theory.

title: Lecture 26 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute.

\(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&4&0\\0&-2&5\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\)

W2. Area scaling. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(\det A\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) go? What area does the unit square map to?
W3. Zero determinant. Explain, in one sentence each, why \(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}=0\) means (i) noninvertible and (ii) the image of the unit square has area zero.
W4. Link to Monday. For invertible \(2\times 2\) \(A\), the formula for \(A^{-1}\) has \(\det A\) in the denominator. What goes wrong if \(\det A=0\)?
W5. Characteristic preview. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), expand \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) as a quadratic in \(\lambda\). (No need to “solve eigenvalues” yet — just form the polynomial.)

title: Lecture 26 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\det\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\2&5&0\\3&1&2\end{bmatrix}\).
Y2. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)\). What is \(|\det A|\)? Interpret as area scaling of the unit square.
Y3. True or false: if \(\det A=0\) for square \(A\), then \(Ax=b\) has either no solution or infinitely many solutions for every \(b\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}=12-(-2)=14\). Lower triangular: \(\det=(-1)(5)(2)=-10\).
Y2. \(|\det A|=|(2)(-1)|=2\): the unit square is mapped to a rectangle of area \(2\) (stretched by \(2\) horizontally and reflected/flipped vertically).
Y3. True. Singular means no unique solution for any \(b\): if \(b\in C(A)\) there are infinitely many solutions; otherwise none.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Learning objectives

Verify a proposed eigenpair.

Connect \(A^t v=\lambda^t v\) to repeated dynamics (powers from Lecture 23).
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Warm-up
Lab 4’s campus matrix (same every week): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.2\\0.3&0.8\end{bmatrix}.
\] You saw \(x_0=(1000,0)\) and \(x_0=(0,1000)\) both head toward about \((400,600)\).

In one sentence: what was surprising?
Preview: if some nonzero \(v\) satisfied \(Av=v\) (eigenvalue \(1\)), why would iterating from that \(v\) stay put (up to scaling of total population)?

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Fill in
Eigenpair. A nonzero vector \(v\) is an eigenvector of square \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) if \[
Av = \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}.
\] Geometrically: \(A\) sends \(v\) to a vector on the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) line through \(v\) (scaled by \(\lambda\); if \(\lambda<0\), also flipped).
Verify. Given a candidate pair \((\lambda,v)\), compute \(Av\) and \(\lambda v\); they must \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
Find \(\lambda\) from \(v\). If \(v\neq 0\) is known to be an eigenvector and some component \(v_i\neq 0\), then \[
\lambda = \frac{(Av)_i}{v_i}
\] (same ratio for every nonzero component).
Dynamics / powers. If \(x_0=v\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), then \[
x_t = A^t v = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] The direction of \(v\) is persistent: each step only rescales (and maybe flips). Lab 4’s long-run mix will turn out to be (a scale of) an eigenvector for \(\lambda=1\); Friday makes that precise.
No real eigenvector. A pure rotation (e.g. \(90^\circ\)) moves every real nonzero vector off its own line. Then there is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) real eigenpair — we will need complex numbers on Wednesday.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Worked in class
W1. Geometry. Sketch \(v=(1,1)\) and \(Av\) for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Is \(v\) an eigenvector? What about \(e_1=(1,0)\)?
W2. Verify. Check whether \((\lambda,v)=(3,(1,1))\) is an eigenpair of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute both \(Av\) and \(\lambda v\).
W3. Find \(\lambda\). You are told that \(v=(1,-1)\) is an eigenvector of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\lambda\). Then confirm \(Av=\lambda v\).
W4. Clean diagonal example (builds intuition for Lab 4). Let \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1.2,\,0.5)\).

Name two real eigenpairs (use the standard basis).
If \(x_0=c_1 e_1+c_2 e_2\), what is \(x_t=B^t x_0\)? Which term dominates for large \(t\) when \(c_1\neq 0\)?

W5. Campus preview. Check that \(v=(2,3)\) is an eigenvector of Lab 4’s \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.2\\0.3&0.8\end{bmatrix}\). What is \(\lambda\)? (Friday: scale to total \(1000\) and match \(x_{20}\).)
W6. Rotation. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW). For a generic \(v=(a,b)\neq 0\), is \(Rv\) a real multiple of \(v\)? What does that say about real eigenvectors of \(R\)?

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Your turn
Y1. Verify or reject: is \((\lambda,v)=(−1,(1,-1))\) an eigenpair of \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)?
Y2. Given that \(v=(1,2)\) is an eigenvector of \(A=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}\), find \(\lambda\).
Y3. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Av=2v\) and \(v\neq 0\), then \(A^3 v=8v\).
Y4. In one sentence: how will an eigenvector for \(\lambda=1\) help explain Lab 4’s “same long-run mix from different starts”?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(Av=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \((-1)v=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Yes — eigenpair.
Y2. \(Av=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}\). Ratio from the first component: \(\lambda=3/1=3\). Check second: \(4=3\cdot 2\). So \(\lambda=3\).
Y3. True. \(A^3 v=A^2(Av)=A^2(2v)=A(4v)=8v\) (or \(A^t v=\lambda^t v\)).
Y4. Sample: A \(\lambda=1\) direction is a steady mix; other modes shrink, so many starts collapse onto (a scale of) that same eigenvector — the long-run campus mix.

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Fill in
Complex numbers. A complex number is \(z=a+bi\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(i^2=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\). Plot \(z\) as the point \((a,b)\) in the complex plane.
Arithmetic (what we need):

Add/subtract: combine real and imaginary parts.
Multiply: \((a+bi)(c+di)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i\).
Conjugate: \(\overline{a+bi}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
Magnitude: \(|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).

Characteristic equation. Eigenvalues of square \(A\) solve \[
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
\] For \(2\times 2\), this is a \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) equation in \(\lambda\).
Eigenvectors. For each eigenvalue \(\lambda\), solve \[
(A-\lambda I)v=0,\qquad v\neq 0
\] (null space of \(A-\lambda I\)). Scale freely — any nonzero multiple is fine.
Check. Always verify \(Av=\lambda v\) by substitution (works for real or complex pairs).

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Worked in class
W1. Complex drill. Let \(z=2+i\) and \(w=1-3i\).

Compute \(z+w\), \(zw\), and \(\overline{z}\).
Plot \(z\) and \(\overline{z}\) in the complex plane.

W2. Real \(2\times 2\) by hand. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Expand \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) and solve for \(\lambda\).
For each eigenvalue, find one eigenvector.
Check one pair by computing \(Av\) and \(\lambda v\).

W3. Rotation eigenvalues. For \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\):

Confirm the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2+1=0\), so \(\lambda=\pm i\).
For \(\lambda=i\), solve \((R-iI)v=0\) and give one complex eigenvector.
Check \(Rv=iv\) by matrix–vector multiplication (complex arithmetic).

W4. Interpretation preview. Complex conjugate eigenvalues of a real matrix often signal \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (rotation / oscillation) in the real plane — Friday’s lab makes this concrete with software.

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \((3-2i)(1+i)\) and \(|3-2i|\).
Y2. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\), find both eigenvalues, and an eigenvector for \(\lambda=3\).
Y3. Check: with \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(v=(1,-i)\), verify \(Av=iv\) (or explain the correct \(\lambda\) if this \(v\) is for \(\lambda=-i\)).
Y4. True or false: every real \(2\times 2\) matrix has two real eigenvalues.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((3-2i)(1+i)=3+3i-2i-2i^2=5+i\). Magnitude: \(|3-2i|=\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}\).
Y2. \(A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}1-\lambda&2\\0&3-\lambda\end{bmatrix}\), so \(\det=(1-\lambda)(3-\lambda)\). Eigenvalues \(\lambda=1\) and \(\lambda=3\). For \(\lambda=3\): \((A-3I)v=\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\0&0\end{bmatrix}v=0\) gives \(v_1=v_2\), e.g. \(v=(1,1)\).
Y3. \(Av=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-i\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}i\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(iv=\begin{bmatrix}i\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Yes — \(Av=iv\) (so this \(v\) matches \(\lambda=i\)).
Y4. False. The characteristic polynomial may have complex roots (e.g. \(90^\circ\) rotation: \(\lambda=\pm i\)).

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad

\] Hand-compute \(Av\). Guess a plausible \(\lambda\) so that \(Av\approx\lambda v\). (Exact eigenpairs come from software in lab.)

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Fill in
Software eigenpairs. Octave eig(A) / Python np.linalg.eig(A) return eigenvalues and a matrix whose columns are eigenvectors.
Verify. For each reported pair \((\lambda,v)\), check \[
Av \approx \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}
\] (componentwise; floating-point noise is expected). Never trust a bare printout without this check.
Dominant behavior. If \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots\) and \(x_0\) has a component along the \(\lambda_1\)-eigenvector, then for large \(t\) \[
A^t x_0 \approx c\,\lambda_1^t\,v_1.
\] That explains Lab 4-style growth/decay/stabilization once you know the eigenpairs.
Complex eigenvalues. For a real matrix, nonreal eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. In the real plane they produce \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (rotation / oscillation), matching Monday’s pure-rotation example.
Normal modes (demo, not a DE course). For a symmetric mass–spring style matrix, eigenvectors are often \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (orthogonal). Software shows the modes; we do not derive differential equations today.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Worked in class
W1. Software sketch. On the board / laptop, for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\):
# Octave:  [V,D] = eig(A)     or    eig(A)
# Python:  vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
Read off \(\lambda\)’s and columns of \(V\). Verify \(A v_1=\lambda_1 v_1\) for one column.
W2. Explain a simulation. Same \(A\) as W1; \(x_0=(1,0)\). Using eigenpairs, explain in one sentence why \(x_t\) grows and which direction it approaches.
W3. Complex / oscillation. Software on \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) should report eigenvalues near \(\pm i\). Connect that to the cycling you saw in Lab 4 stretch / Lecture 35.
W4. Symmetric demo. Let \(S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) (symmetric). Check that the two eigenvectors from W1 are orthogonal (\(v_1^{\mathsf{T}}v_2=0\)). Normal-mode pictures use the same idea in higher dimension.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Your turn
Y1. Pseudocode: given \(A\), obtain eigenpairs in software and write the one-line check that \(Av\approx\lambda v\) for the first pair.
Y2. True or false: if \(|\lambda_1|=1.5\) and \(|\lambda_2|=0.5\), then for generic \(x_0\) the long-run direction of \(A^t x_0\) is the \(\lambda_1\)-eigendirection.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Sample: vals, V = np.linalg.eig(A) then A @ V[:,0] - vals[0]*V[:,0] (should be near \(0\)); Octave: [V,D]=eig(A) then A*V(:,1) - D(1,1)*V(:,1).
Y2. True. The \(\lambda_1\) term grows relative to \(\lambda_2\), so the state aligns with \(v_1\) (unless the \(v_1\)-component of \(x_0\) is exactly zero).

text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) as the orthogonal projection of \(b\) onto \(C(A)\).
Interpret the residual \(r=b-\hat{b}\) as orthogonal to \(C(A)\) at a minimizer.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Warm-up
Consider the overdetermined system \(Ax=b\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

How many equations? How many unknowns? Is \(A\) tall, wide, or square?
Suppose someone guesses \(x=(1,0.5)\). Compute \(Ax\) and \(Ax-b\). Is \(x\) an exact solution?

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Fill in
Overdetermined / inconsistent. When there are more independent equations than unknowns, \(Ax=b\) often has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) exact solution. The right-hand side \(b\) may lie outside the column space \(C(A)\).
Least-squares idea. Instead of insisting on \(Ax=b\), choose \(\hat{x}\) to make \(A\hat{x}\) as close as possible to \(b\): \[
\hat{x}\;=\;\arg\min_x\;\lVert Ax-b\rVert.
\] The vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) attainable right-hand side in \(C(A)\).
Projection picture. Among all vectors in the subspace \(C(A)\), the closest one to \(b\) is the orthogonal projection of \(b\) onto \(C(A)\). Least squares is exactly that geometry in disguise: \[
\hat{b}\;=\;\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b),\qquad
\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\text{ for some }\hat{x}.
\] (So \(\hat{x}\) are the coordinates of that projection in the columns of \(A\).)
Recall — orthogonal vectors (Lecture 4). Two vectors \(u,v\) are orthogonal when their inner product is zero: \(u^{\mathsf{T}}v=0\) (a right angle). Same vocabulary as early in the semester; now one vector is the residual and the other lives in \(C(A)\).
Residual. The residual is \[
r = b - A\hat{x} = b - \hat{b}
\] (some texts write \(A\hat{x}-b\); same length \(\|r\|\)). At a minimizer, \(r\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) to every vector in \(C(A)\): for every column \(a_j\) of \(A\), \[
a_j^{\mathsf{T}}r = \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}.
\] (That stack of \(n\) equations is \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r=0\) — Wednesday’s bridge to the normal equations.)
Exact vs approximate.







Situation
Meaning




Exact solution
\(Ax=b\) for some \(x\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(b\in\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(\hat{b}=b\)


Least-squares solution
\(\hat{b}=\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b)\); residual may be \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)



If an exact solution exists, it is also a least-squares solution (residual zero — \(b\) already lives in \(C(A)\)).

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Worked in class
W1. Inconsistent check. For the warm-up \(A\) and \(b\), argue that no \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) can satisfy all three equations simultaneously. (Hint: equations 1–2 force \(x_2=1\); plug into equation 3.)
W2. Objective value. With the same \(A,b\) and trial \(x=(1,0.5)\), compute \(\|Ax-b\|\) (Euclidean). Is this the minimum? (You need not prove optimality yet — just evaluate the objective.)
W3. Projection sketch. Sketch (in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) as a cartoon, or think in words): \(C(A)\) is a plane (or line) through the origin; \(b\) is off the plane; \(\hat{b}=\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b)\) is the foot of the perpendicular. Label \(r=b-\hat{b}\) and mark the right angle between \(r\) and the plane — same “\(u^{\mathsf{T}}v=0\)” idea as Lecture 4, now between \(r\) and every direction in \(C(A)\).
W4. Exact case. Change \(b\) to \(b'=(1,2,3)\). Show that \(x=(1,1)\) solves \(Ax=b'\) exactly. What is the residual? What is \(\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b')\) in this case?
W5. Language check. In one sentence each: (i) “no exact solution,” (ii) “\(\hat{b}\) is the projection of \(b\) onto \(C(A)\).”

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) and \(r=b-Ax\). Is \(x\) an exact solution? What is \(\|r\|\)?
Y2. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Ax=b\) is inconsistent, then no vector \(\hat{x}\) can make \(\|A\hat{x}-b\|\) finite.
Y3. In words: why do we call \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) the orthogonal projection of \(b\) onto \(C(A)\)?
Y4. A \(4\times 2\) matrix \(A\) has linearly independent columns, and \(b\notin C(A)\). Can \(Ax=b\) have an exact solution? Can it have a least-squares solution? What is \(\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b)\) equal to in that case — \(b\), or something else?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(Ax=(2,1,1)\); \(r=(1,0,0)\); not exact. \(\|r\|=1\).
Y2. False. The residual norm is always finite; least squares still chooses an \(\hat{x}\) that minimizes it (even when the minimum is positive).
Y3. It is the unique closest point in \(C(A)\) to \(b\), and the error \(b-\hat{b}\) is orthogonal to every vector in \(C(A)\) in the Lecture 4 sense (\(u^{\mathsf{T}}v=0\)) — that is the definition of orthogonal projection onto \(C(A)\).
Y4. Exact: no (\(b\notin C(A)\)). Least squares: yes. Here \(\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b)=\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\neq b\) (something else — the foot of the perpendicular in \(C(A)\)).

text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Check the residual’s orthogonality to the columns of \(A\).

Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, explain \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=\lVert Ax\rVert^2\), and recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is positive definite when \(A\) has linearly independent columns.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Warm-up
Monday: \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}=\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b)\), so the residual \(r=b-\hat{b}\) is orthogonal to every column of \(A\) in the Lecture 4 sense: each \(a_j^{\mathsf{T}}r=0\). Stacked, that is \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r=0\), which rearranges to the normal equations \[
A^{\mathsf{T}}A\,\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b.
\]

If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) with \(m>n\), what size is \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\)? Why is that nicer than solving \(Ax=b\) directly?
True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always symmetric.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Fill in
From projection to algebra (no calculus). “\(r\perp C(A)\)” means \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r=0\). Substitute \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) to get \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b\). So the normal equations are the algebraic form of the projection picture — we never need derivatives of \(\|Ax-b\|^2\); the Lecture 4 right-angle condition is enough.
Normal equations / software. Solving \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (when \(A\) has independent columns) gives the unique least-squares \(\hat{x}\). In practice we often call a solver instead of forming \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) by hand:








Task
Octave
Python




Least-squares \(\hat{x}\)
xhat = A \ b
xhat = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]


Fitted values
bhat = A*xhat
bhat = A @ xhat


Residual
r = b - bhat
r = b - bhat


RMS
rms = norm(r)/sqrt(m)
rms = np.linalg.norm(r)/np.sqrt(m)



Orthogonality check. At a least-squares solution, \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r \approx \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (numerical noise ok).
RMS. Root-mean-square residual \(\mathrm{RMS}=\|r\|/\sqrt{m}\) reports a typical per-equation error in the same units as \(b\).
Useful vs coefficients. Always ask: do fitted values track the data? Is RMS small in context? Blindly quoting \(\hat{x}\) is not enough.
Basis choice = columns of \(A\) (Lecture 14 vocabulary). A “nice” curve is often approximated by a finite combination of basis functions. Two useful choices:








Basis idea
Typical columns of \(A\) (one row per sample \(t_i\))
Good for




Monomials
\(1\), \(t\), \(t^2\), 
Smooth global trends (polynomials)


Truncated powers (order 1)
\(1\), \(t\), \((t-\xi)_+\) where \((t-\xi)_+=\max(t-\xi,0)\)
A kink / change of slope at a knot \(\xi\)



Same LS projection onto \(C(A)\) either way — you just changed the subspace by changing the basis. Higher-order truncated powers \((t-\xi)_+^k\) exist; we only need the picture that “turn on after \(\xi\)” can beat a global polynomial when the data bend once.
Neural networks (one honest sentence). A ReLU unit is the truncated-linear ray \((z)_+=\max(z,0)\). With a bias, \(\operatorname{ReLU}(t-\xi)=\max(t-\xi,0)\) is exactly our order-\(1\) truncated power with knot \(\xi\) — the bias chooses where the ray starts. In a network those knots / directions are data-driven (learned), then combined with coefficients, just as we combine columns of \(A\) in least squares. Stacking enough such ReLU features is a standard route to universal approximation: rich enough ramp bases can approximate a wide class of nice functions. We will not prove that theorem; the takeaway is that “choose a basis, fit coefficients” is the same skeleton — monomials, fixed knots, or learned ReLU biases.
Where this shows up in the news. Large language models such as ChatGPT are built from neural networks. The “T” in GPT stands for Transformer — a particular network architecture (attention layers stacked deep), not a different kind of mathematics. Same broad idea: learned features + linear combinations at enormous scale. We will not study Transformers in this course.
Positive semidefinite / definite (Boyd / class notes). A symmetric matrix \(P\) is positive semidefinite (PSD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px\ge 0\) for all \(x\); positive definite (PD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px>0\) for all \(x\neq 0\).
For any \(A\): \[
x^{\mathsf{T}}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)x = \lVert Ax\rVert^2 \ge 0,
\] so \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\). It is positive definite precisely when \(Ax=0\Rightarrow x=0\), i.e. when \(A\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) columns — then the normal equations have a unique solution.

text:
Worked in class
W1. Tiny fit by hand / software. Four campus shuttle wait times (minutes) at hours \(t=1,2,3,4\) after 8am: \[
b=(6,\,7,\,10,\,11).
\] Model a line \(b\approx x_1 + x_2 t\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Form \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (or use A\b / lstsq).
Report \(\hat{x}=(x_1,x_2)\) and the fitted values \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\).
Compute \(r\) and RMS. In one sentence: is a linear trend reasonable here?

Expected (for checking): \(\hat{x}=(4,\,1.8)\) exactly from the normal equations; \(\hat{b}=(5.8,\,7.6,\,9.4,\,11.2)\); RMS \(=\sqrt{0.2}\approx 0.45\) minutes.
W2. Orthogonality. With your \(\hat{x}\) from W1, compute \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\). Should it be near \((0,0)\)?
W3. Plot story. On axes “hour \(t\)” vs “wait (min)”, sketch data points and the fitted line. Where is the residual for \(t=1\) visible?
W4. PSD identity. Expand \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax\) for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) and a general \(x=(x_1,x_2)\). Confirm it equals \(\|Ax\|^2\) and is \(\ge 0\).
W5. PD vs PSD. Explain why \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) fails to be positive definite if the two columns of \(A\) are equal. What goes wrong for uniqueness of \(\hat{x}\)?
W6. Truncated power vs monomials. Five samples \(t=1,2,3,4,5\) with responses \[
b=(2,\,2.2,\,2.4,\,5,\,7)
\] (almost flat, then steeper after \(t=3\)).

Build the line model: columns \(1\) and \(t\). (Optional: glance at RMS after lstsq.)
Build a truncated-power model with knot \(\xi=3\): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1&1&0\\
1&2&0\\
1&3&0\\
1&4&1\\
1&5&2
\end{bmatrix}
\] (columns \(1\), \(t\), \((t-3)_+\)). Solve for \(\hat{x}\) and compare RMS to the line. Which subspace matches the kink better?

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Your turn
Y1. Using the W1 data, suppose software returns \(\hat{x}=(4,\,1.8)\). Compute \(\hat{b}_1=x_1+x_2\cdot 1\) and the first residual \(r_1=b_1-\hat{b}_1\).
Y2. True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always positive definite for every \(A\).
Y3. Why check \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\approx 0\) after a least-squares solve?
Y4. A fit has RMS \(=0.02\) °C for outdoor temperature data that typically varies by \(10\) °C across the day. Useful model, or not? One sentence.
Y5. In one sentence: what does switching from monomials to a truncated-power column change — the LS geometry, or the model subspace \(C(A)\)?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(\hat{b}_1=4+1.8=5.8\); \(r_1=6-5.8=0.2\).
Y2. False. \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always PSD, but PD only when \(A\) has linearly independent columns (equivalently \(\ker A=\{0\}\)).
Y3. It is the normal-equation / geometric check that the residual is orthogonal to \(C(A)\) — evidence that \(\hat{x}\) really is a least-squares critical point (up to roundoff).
Y4. Useful in context: RMS \(\ll\) the natural scale of the data, so typical pointwise error is tiny compared with day-scale variation.
Y5. The LS geometry is the same (project \(b\) onto \(C(A)\)); what changes is the choice of subspace — different basis columns mean a different \(C(A)\).

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Fill in
SVD (conceptual). Every real \(m\times n\) matrix factors as \[
A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}},
\] where the columns of \(U\) and \(V\) are orthonormal (left / right singular vectors) and \(\Sigma\) is rectangular “diagonal” with nonnegative singular values \[
\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge 0
\] on its main diagonal. Think: \(A\) = rotate/reflect → stretch by \(\sigma_i\) → rotate/reflect.
Factorizations in this course. Lab 3 introduced a first useful factorization: \(A=LU\) (elimination saved as a product — built to solve \(Ax=b\)). Today’s SVD is a second: built from orthonormal directions and singular values — built to approximate, compress, and compute least squares stably.
Orthonormal payoff (Lecture 14). “Orthonormal” still means \(q_i^{\mathsf{T}}q_j=0\) for \(i\neq j\) and \(\|q_i\|=1\). The SVD hands you orthonormal bases (columns of \(U\) and of \(V\)). That is why those bases were worth defining earlier: coordinates via inner products, and this factorization, both use them.
Two jobs for SVD. (1) Stable LS: the LS solution is still \(\hat{b}=\operatorname{proj}_{C(A)}(b)\) (Lectures 38–39); SVD is a reliable way to compute \(\hat{x}\) (software’s lstsq often uses this family). (2) Compression: keep only the largest \(\sigma_i\) for a rank-\(k\) picture (capstone).
Callback — eigenvectors (Lectures 35–37, Lab 5). Eigenvectors name directions that \(A\) only rescales (\(Av=\lambda v\)); the largest \(|\lambda|\) wins the long run. Singular vectors / singular values name directions that \(A\) stretches the most (\(\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\)). Different jobs, same “keep the dominant directions” instinct: Lab 5’s \(\lambda=1\) mode vs today’s keep-large-\(\sigma_i\) compression. (For square symmetric cases the two stories are closely related; we do not need that theorem to use either tool.)
Rank-\(k\) approximation. Keep the largest \(k\) singular values (and matching singular-vector columns); set the rest to zero. The truncated product \[
A_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^{\mathsf{T}}
\] is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in the usual 2-norm / Frobenius sense (details in the slides / capstone). Same idea as “keep the important orthonormal directions.”
Software sketch (lab / capstone):








Task
Octave
Python




SVD
[U,S,V] = svd(A)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)


Rank-\(k\) rebuild
use first \(k\) columns / \(\sigma\)’s
U[:,:k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k,:]


Least squares
A\b
np.linalg.lstsq(A,b,rcond=None)[0]

Plan

title: Capstone — Low-rank frames vs differences
text:
Technical notes
Storage (order of magnitude).

One full frame: \(mn\) numbers.
One rank-\(k\) factorization: about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers (columns of \(U_k\), \(V_k\), and \(k\) singular values).
Plan A total (three frames): about \(3k(m+n+1)\).
Plan B total (three matrices): also about \(3k(m+n+1)\) at the same \(k\) — so Plan B wins on storage only if you can use a smaller \(k\) for differences while matching Plan A’s error, or if you choose different \(k\) per matrix on purpose.

Error. For a matrix \(A\) and approximation \(A_k\), a standard relative Frobenius error is \[
\frac{\lVert A-A_k\rVert_F}{\lVert A\rVert_F}.
\] Under Plan B, measure error on the reconstructed frames \(\widehat F_2=\widehat F_1+\widehat D_2\), etc., not only on the difference matrices.

2 & 4 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.

\(A\) is invertible

\(\det A\neq 0\)


\(N(A)=\{0\}\)

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.

This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

Late or Missed Work Policies
The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Lecture attendance is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 lecture days without penalty and without contacting me. Reserve these days for emergencies. In my experience, it is rare for a student to succeed if they regularly miss class or are absent for more than two weeks, so if you find yourself in that situation, please communicate with me and your advisor so we can help you find a solution.
Quizzes are in the first 10 minutes of class. The lowest two quiz scores are dropped. If you must miss a quiz due to illness or another emergency, please contact me to arrange a makeup.
Labs are credited in class on the dates on the schedule: complete the hub exercises, handwrite the one-pager, and get initials. After a week, missed lab credit is not made up except by arrangement (e.g. illness).
